n: Samuel privately anoints Saul by pouring oil on his head and kisses him in respect. Anointing set someone apart for a sacred calling by God's authority.

f.g: a small flask of olive oil
Anointing with oil symbolized being chosen and empowered by God.

n: Samuel gives three signs to confirm the anointing. First, near Rachel's tomb two men will tell Saul the donkeys are found and that his father is now worried about him.
Second, at the oak of Tabor he will meet three men going to worship at Bethel, carrying goats, bread, and wine for an offering.

f.g: Better “oak of Tabor,” a landmark tree; not Mount Tabor in Galilee.

n: They will greet him and give him two loaves of bread, which he should accept — perhaps a hint that he is already being honored as a leader.
Third, at the “hill of God,” near a Philistine outpost, he will meet a group of prophets coming down from worship with music, prophesying.

f.g: A group of people who worshipped together and were moved by the Spirit, sometimes called “sons of the prophets.”
a stringed instrument like a lyre

n: The Spirit of the Lord will come on Saul, he will prophesy with them, and he will be changed into a different man. God equips those He calls.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD will come upon thee

n: Once the signs happen, Saul should act as the situation requires, knowing God is with him.
Samuel gives Saul an important instruction: go to Gilgal and wait seven days until Samuel comes to offer sacrifices. This command becomes a test of Saul's obedience later.
As Saul turns to leave, God gives him a new heart, and every sign comes true that very day.
At the hill, the group of prophets meets Saul, the Spirit of God comes on him, and he prophesies with them, just as Samuel foretold.
Those who knew Saul are amazed to see him prophesying and ask what has happened to Kish's son. “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

f.w: Is Saul also among the prophets?

n: Someone asks, “Who is their father?” — perhaps meaning prophecy is a gift from God, not something inherited. The question became a common saying for an unexpected change in someone.
When the prophesying ends, Saul goes up to the high place to worship.
Saul's uncle asks where they had been. Saul says they were looking for the donkeys and went to Samuel when they could not find them.
His uncle is curious about what Samuel told them.
Saul tells only that the donkeys were found and keeps the news about the kingdom to himself — perhaps out of humility or caution.
Samuel gathers the whole nation at Mizpeh to publicly choose the king before the Lord.
Samuel speaks for the Lord, reminding Israel of how He freed them from Egypt and all their oppressors.

f.w: I brought up Israel out of Egypt

n: Yet they have rejected God, their true Savior, by demanding a king. Still, God will grant it. Samuel tells them to present themselves by tribes and clans for selection.

f.w: ye have this day rejected your God

n: The tribes come forward and the tribe of Benjamin is chosen, probably by casting lots, which Israel believed God controlled.
Narrowing down by family, the lot falls on Matri's clan and then on Saul himself. But when they look for him, he is nowhere to be found.
They ask the Lord where he is, and the answer is almost humorous: he is hiding among the baggage. Saul's shyness or fear shows here.
They bring him out, and he stands a head taller than everyone. Outwardly he looks every bit a king.

f.w: higher than any of the people

n: Samuel presents him as the Lord's chosen, unmatched among the people, and the crowd shouts, “God save the king!” — literally, “Let the king live!”
Samuel explains the rights and duties of the kingship and writes them in a book kept before the Lord. Even the king would be under God's law.
Saul goes home to Gibeah, joined by valiant men whose hearts God had moved to support him.

f.g: Saul's hometown in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem; it became his capital.

n: Some troublemakers scorn Saul, doubt he can save them, and refuse to bring gifts of loyalty. Saul wisely says nothing — a moment of self-control.
